'''James Ashley Donaldson''' (April 17, 1941 — October 18, 2019) was an American mathematician.  He was a professor at [[Howard University]], where he was instrumental in establishing a PhD program in mathematics.  He also helped found the [[National Association of Mathematicians]].

==Education and career==
Donaldson was born in on April 17, 1941, on a farm near [[Tallahassee, Florida]], where he grew up attending [[segregated school]]s.<ref name="notices">{{cite journal | last1=Hunt | first1=Fern Y | last2=Wilson | first2=Robin T | last3=Williams | first3=Daniel A | last4=Gray | first4=Mary | last5=Davis | first5=Chandler | last6=Herron | first6=Isom | last7=Brooks | first7=Sean | title=James A. Donaldson — Black Mathematician, Advocate, Gentleman (1941–2019) | journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society | publisher=American Mathematical Society (AMS) | volume=68 | issue=2 | date=2021-02-01 | page=1 | issn=0002-9920 | doi=10.1090/noti2222 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/james-donaldson|work=The HistoryMakers|date=March 28, 2013|title=Interview with James Donaldson}}</ref>  In the wake of [[Brown v. Board of Education]], he took the advice of his high school mathematics teacher to attend college in the [[northern United States]], where he attended [[Lincoln University (Pennsylvania)|Lincoln University]] in [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name="lincolnobit">{{cite web|url=https://www.lincoln.edu/news-and-events/news/lincoln-university-celebrates-life-dr-james-donaldson-%E2%80%9961-educator-and|title=Lincoln University Celebrates The Life Of Dr. James A. Donaldson '61, Educator And Mathematician|work=News|publisher=Lincoln University|date=October 23, 2019|access-date=January 23, 2021|archive-date=January 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210129092615/https://www.lincoln.edu/news-and-events/news/lincoln-university-celebrates-life-dr-james-donaldson-%E2%80%9961-educator-and|url-status=dead}}</ref>  After graduating from Lincoln with a AB in mathematics in 1961, he moved to the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] for his graduate work, where he completed an MS degree in 1963, and a PhD in 1965.<ref name="notices"/><ref name="maa">{{cite web|url=https://www.maa.org/james-ashley-donaldson|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|title=James Ashley Donaldson|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>  His PhD thesis on [[partial differential equations]] was titled ''Integral Representations of the Extended Airy Integral Type for the Modified Bessel Function'', and was supervised by Ray Gartner Langebartel.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=951|name=James Ashley Donaldson}}</ref>

Following his PhD, Donaldson had short term appointments at [[Southern University]], [[Howard University]], the [[University of Illinois at Chicago]], and the [[University of New Mexico]].<ref name="maa"/>  He returned to Howard University in 1971 as a professor, where he remained for most of the rest of his career.<ref name="howardobit">{{cite web|url=https://newsroom.howard.edu/newsroom/article/11391/celebrating-life-james-donaldson-phd|work=Newsroom|publisher=Howard University|date=October 21, 2019|access-date=January 23, 2021|title=Celebrating the Life of James A. Donaldson, Ph.D.}}</ref>  He served as chair of the mathematics department at Howard from 1972 until 1990, in which role he was instrumental in developing a PhD program in mathematics.  Howard's program, established in 1976, was the first PhD program in mathematics at a [[historically black college or university]].<ref name="notices"/><ref name="howardobit"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ortega|first1=Omayra|last2=Lawrence|first2=Emille Davie |last3=Goins|first3=Edray Herber|title=The Golden Anniversary Celebration of the National Association of Mathematicians|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jsQOEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA177|date=10 December 2020|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-1-4704-5130-1|page=177}}</ref>  In the 1998—1999 school year, Donaldson took a leave of absence from Howard to serve as the acting president of Lincoln University, his undergraduate alma mater.<ref name="lincolnobit"/><ref name="jbhe"/>  He returned to Howard in 1999, and from that year until 2012 he served as dean of the College of Arts and Sciences.<ref name="notices"/><ref name="howardobit"/>  Donaldson retired and was granted emeritus status in 2013.<ref name="jbhe">{{cite journal|url=https://www.jbhe.com/2019/10/in-memoriam-james-a-donaldson-1941-2019/|journal=Journal of Blacks in Higher Education|date=October 29, 2019|title=In Memoriam: James A. Donaldson, 1941-2019|access-date=January 23, 2021}}</ref>

==Organizational work==
In 1969, Donaldson was one of the founding members of the [[National Association of Mathematicians]], the professional society promoting mathematical development of underrepresented minorities.  He served as the first editor of the newsletter of that organization, and was a member of its board of directors from 1984 to 1994.<ref name="notices"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ortega|first1=Omayra|last2=Lawrence|first2=Emille Davie |last3=Goins|first3=Edray Herber|title=The Golden Anniversary Celebration of the National Association of Mathematicians|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jsQOEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA7|date=10 December 2020|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-1-4704-5130-1|pages=7–9}}</ref>

==Death==
Donaldson died of heart disease on October 18, 2019, at his home in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name="notices" /><ref name="jbhe"/>

==Awards and honors==
In 2018, Donaldson received an honorary doctoral degree from his former undergraduate institution, Lincoln University.<ref name="notices"/><ref name="lincolnobit"/>  In 2021, a Special Session in Donaldson's honor was held at the [[Joint Mathematics Meetings]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jointmathematicsmeetings.org//meetings/national/jmm2021/2247_program_ss78.html|title=AMS-NAM Joint Special Session on Celebrating the Mathematical Legacy of Dr. James A. Donaldson|website=Joint Mathematics Meetings|date=January 2021}}</ref>
